title: Security posture discovery with Fjord Analytics
summary: Intro discovery on security posture and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer is SOC2-ready, wants clarification around SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, KMS integration, and data retention policies. Agreed to run a short security questionnaire and schedule a dedicated architecture review with their infra team.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC2/ISO attestation + security whitepaper (Maya)
Customer to complete security questionnaire and share network diagram (Lena)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-07
Time: 15:00 - 15:34 UTC
Duration: 34 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), David Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood CSM); Lena Park (CISO, Fjord), Arjun Mehta (VP Eng), Samira Khan (Platform Lead), Gary Luo (SRE)

Summary (auto): quick intro, current stack + security posture, deep dive into SSO/RBAC/audit logs/KMS, agreement to share artifacts and follow-up architecture call.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, with David our solutions engineer and Priya from customer success. How are you all?
[00:06] Lena Park: Good, thanks Maya. Appreciate you fitting us in, we've been evaluating a few inference platforms, security is a big gating factor for us.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Totally, that's what we want to cover today — specifically SOC2/ISO posture, SSO and SAML flows, RBAC and audit logging, and encryption/KMS and retention. Quick for context, Arjun could you share your current infra?
[00:23] Arjun Mehta: Sure, we run a hybrid cloud setup. Prod lives in GCP, some batch in AWS. We're using GKE for our platform and Vault for secrets; we already have SAML SSO via Okta.
[00:31] David Ortiz: Great. When teams think about Redwood we usually frame three deployment modes — Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Hosted is our managed API with shared tenancy but strong tenant isolation and SOC2 controls; Dedicated is reserved GPU pools for a customer in our infra; Private is a VPC-forward private control plane or fully private on-prem.
[00:47] Samira Khan: Can you expand on the difference from a security/audit perspective?
[00:50] Maya Chen: Yeah, hosted still gives you SOC2 controls, encryption at rest and in transit, audit logs surfaced in the console, but data logically lives in our environment. Dedicated gives dedicated capacity and stronger network isolation; logs are still available but you can configure retention. Private (VPC) gives you customer-managed networking, option for on-prem or VPC peering, and tighter controls — often customers ask for KMS/HSM integration here.
[01:14] Lena Park: We're SOC2 type II in progress internally; one of our requirements is that vendors either have SOC2 or can support an attestation and provide compensating controls. Do you have SOC2?
[01:24] Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood is SOC2 Type II. We'll send the report and the summary redacted version. We also maintain an ISO 27001 summary; I'll include that in the pack.
[01:33] Lena Park: Good. For SSO, we use Okta. We need SAML-based SSO for the console and SCIM for provisioning. What's supported?
[01:42] David Ortiz: We support SAML 2.0 for the console SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. There's a few caveats with roles — our RBAC maps IdP groups to Redwood roles; we can map Okta groups to admin/editor/viewer. There are some edge cases for fine-grained permissions where customers request custom roles, we can handle via our enterprise RBAC in Private or Dedicated deployments.
[02:03] Samira Khan: What about session duration and SSO session timeouts? We need SSO sessions to respect our SSO timeout policies.
[02:09] David Ortiz: We do respect SAML assertions and can align session timeouts to the IdP settings; for longer sessions we issue short-lived tokens and refresh. Exact TTLs we can discuss with infra during the architecture review.
[02:20] Gary Luo: Audit logs — how granular are they? We need user-level actions, API calls, model deployments, prompt/response access logs. Also retention policy, and the ability to export logs to our SIEM (Splunk) or to a GCS bucket.
[02:33] Maya Chen: We capture user actions, API request metadata, model version changes, and admin changes. For Hosted we surface logs via the console and provide export APIs; we can push logs to customer-owned cloud storage or to SIEMs via connectors. Retention is configurable depending on plan — enterprise customers can set longer retention.
[02:48] Lena Park: Do you have WORM or immutable logs? For audit we might need tamper-evident logs.
[02:53] David Ortiz: We support append-only audit logs with signed entries in Dedicated and Private deployments. For Hosted we have tamper-evident controls and can offer attestations; if stricter immutability is required, Private with customer-managed storage is recommended.
[03:08] Arjun Mehta: Encryption — at rest and in transit is expected. Can we use our own KMS keys? We need to manage keys in Vault/GCP KMS.
[03:16] Maya Chen: Yes. We support customer-managed keys (CMKs) for Dedicated and Private. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and integrate with major cloud KMS providers; for highest control Private deployment lets you bring your own HSM/KMS and keep keys in your account.
[03:29] Samira Khan: How about data retention and prompt logging — we want to avoid storing sensitive PII from prompts. Can we disable prompt logging or configure redaction?
[03:36] David Ortiz: We provide options: you can disable storing request bodies for retention shorter windows, configure automatic redaction rules, or route logs to customer storage without retention on Redwood. For Hosted there are default retention policies but enterprise customers can request custom SLAs.
[03:51] Lena Park: What about data residency? We must ensure data for EU users stays in EU regions.
[03:57] Maya Chen: Region pinning is supported. Hosted has region selection, and Dedicated/Private can be deployed in customer-preferred regions to meet residency requirements. We'll include our region coverage doc.
[04:08] Gary Luo: Compliance/certificates — other than SOC2/ISO, do you have penetration test reports or third-party assessments?
[04:14] Maya Chen: We run regular third-party pentests and vulnerability scans; we can share summary findings and attestations under an NDA. Also incident response playbooks and SLAs for incident notification.
[04:25] Samira Khan: Network connectivity — for Private we'd want VPC peering and allowlist of Redwood IPs for Dedicated. For Hosted, is there a way to set IP allowlist?
[04:34] David Ortiz: Hosted has IP allowlisting for API keys and can integrate with customer IP restrictions. Dedicated and Private support direct peering and private connectivity. We'll go over the network diagrams in the next call.
[04:47] Arjun Mehta: Pricing compliance question — is there a difference in data handling between paid Dedicated and the hosted tiers?
[04:53] Maya Chen: Functionally similar controls, but Dedicated gives you dedicated compute and stronger network isolation. Private gives you full control. There are contractual differences like data handling clauses and SLAs which we can include in the procurement security pack.
[05:05] Lena Park: Ok, next — incident response and breach notification timelines? We need 72-hour notification and details on forensic logs access.
[05:13] Priya Desai: We typically commit to 72-hour initial notification as part of enterprise contracts; more details and playbooks we can provide. Forensics access to logs depends on deployment; Private gives direct access, Dedicated can provide expanded log access, Hosted provides exports and SOC team support.
[05:30] Samira Khan: For RBAC, can we do least-privilege for models — e.g., restrict who can deploy model weights vs who can call inference endpoints?
[05:36] David Ortiz: Yes, RBAC is role-based and you can separate deployment permissions from runtime invocation. In Private and Dedicated you can get very fine-grained controls; Hosted covers common roles but custom roles are available under enterprise setups.
[05:50] Gary Luo: API keys vs token rotation — how often should keys rotate, do you support short-lived tokens and automated rotation?
[05:58] David Ortiz: We support short-lived tokens, OAuth flows, and automated rotation via our SDK; we recommend rotating keys every 90 days by default, but you can adopt stricter policies.
[06:08] Lena Park: Let's talk about the tech deep-dive — we want to run a bench of our most common inference workloads to measure latency and to validate that prompt data does not leak across customers. How do you handle KV cache isolation?
[06:19] David Ortiz: Isolation is strict — KV caches are per-model-instance and per-tenant. For Dedicated we provision per-customer pools. For Hosted we have multi-tenant isolation with strict logical boundaries. We'll include a security note on KV cache handling.
[06:33] Arjun Mehta: For the bench, can we run a pilot where we send a subset of traffic and measure? We prefer a canary approach.
[06:39] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We can do a POC with limited data, or synthetic traces. If you want to test with live data, Private or Dedicated is often used. We'll define scope with the engineering team in the follow-up.
[06:52] Lena Park: Any common gotchas you've seen?
[06:55] David Ortiz: A few: network egress patterns for hosted APIs, token TTL alignment with Okta, and explicit requirements for KMS bring-your-own-key in on-prem setups. Also audit log retention defaults differ by plan so it's important to confirm SLAs.
[07:10] Samira Khan: For forensic requests, what's the turnaround for log exports?
[07:14] Priya Desai: We typically can export logs within 24-48 hours for enterprise agreements; for immediate access Private will give you direct access.
[07:23] Lena Park: Ok this is helpful. Can you outline what you'll send over after this call?
[07:27] Maya Chen: We'll send: SOC2 Type II report (redacted), ISO summary, security whitepaper, network diagram template, security questionnaire, and a proposed agenda for an architecture deep-dive.
[07:36] Arjun Mehta: We'll fill the questionnaire and propose times for the deep-dive next week.
[07:40] Maya Chen: Great. Any final quick questions?
[07:43] Gary Luo: One last — do you support redact-on-ingress for PII?
[07:47] David Ortiz: We have redaction pipelines you can enable; for strict requirements use Private or choose to route request payloads to customer storage.
[07:55] Lena Park: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[07:57] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the pack.
[08:00] -- End of call --

Notes: transcript contains occasional transcription errors and shorthand; timestamps approximate every 15-60s throughout a 34 minute call.
